Opinion 1: 22. Kratom is not and should not be characterized as “an opioid,” nor regulated as a dangerous or addictive controlled substance in the United States Controlled Substances Act (“CSA”) or under the International Drug Control Conventions of United Nations. I agree with the determinations of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services (“DHHS”), DEA and the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (“UNODC”) that kratom does not warrant such designations or control. Opinion 2: 23. Kratom is not characterized by “high abuse,” “dependence” or “addiction” potential and is well within the range of many licit consumer dietary substances and health products (e.g., caffeine, antihistamines, and CBD) that are abused and can be addictive in some people but overall are used primarily for their beneficial and otherwise useful health and/or life-enhancing effects. Opinion 3: 24. Kratom does not carry a high risk of death. To the contrary, the risk of death by kratom alone appears very low and rare. This has also been the conclusion of NIDA and DEA for approximately a decade and similarly concluded by FDA in 2024 after its approximately decade of review and own testing. My opinion continues to be consistent with Assistant Secretary Gior’s 2018 review statement on this matter: “There is still debate among reputable scientists over whether kratom by itself is associated with fatal overdoses.” Opinion 4: 25. There is no consensus on the basis by which kratom might cause life threatening effects or death; in contrast to most substances that contribute to overdose deaths (e.g., respiratory depression by opioids and sedatives, cardiovascular incidents by stimulants). Opinion 5: 26. There is no consensus on what level of kratom consumption or level in the bloodstream would constitute a lethal dose, in contrast to most substances of high abuse, addiction and mortality potential that contribute to the U.S. drug overdose epidemic. Specifically, there is no well-defined toxidrome for kratom, but rather kratom associated deaths most commonly involve other substances, including prescription and non-prescribed drugs, and various pre-existing disease conditions. Deaths occurring in the absence of use of other substances are rare, as concluded by NIDA (2022) and FDA (2024). Opinion 6: 5

OPINIONS SPECIFIC TO PLAINTIFFS’ CLAIMS 35. In this section I provide opinions specific to Plaintiff’s allegations. 36. Plaintiff has not provided valid and reliable support for the allegation that kratom was the cause, or a substantial contributing factor, to Harmony Moller’s death on February 6, 2023. 37. The coroner’s report, as cited in the Complaint (para 33), suggests potential pre- existing heart abnormalities, e.g., “Abnormally high left coronary ostia takeoff.” The coroner’s report does not provide a basis for concluding that mitragynine contributed to Ms. Moller’s death. I note that blood levels of mitragynine were far lower than those that are sometimes associated with death (150 ng/mL by NMS Labs and 158 ng/mL by UC). NMS labs did not find a positive result for the mitragynine metabolite, 7-hydroxymitragynine (“7-OH”), which is consistent with low kratom/mitragynine intake. However, the NMS Labs reports did identify several other pharmacological substances and metabolites. 38. Although I do not have an opinion on the actual cause of Ms. Moller’s death, my scientific training and experience make clear that singling out kratom use as the primary or substantial contributor to death is confounded by Ms. Moller’s potential preexisting conditions and other substance use. 39. The autopsy finding that Ms. Moller’s pre-existing heart condition was “exacerbated by Mitragynine use” is speculative. There is no established scientific or medical consensus that mitragynine “exacerbates” Ms. Moller’s specific and rare cardiac anomaly or causes death in such circumstances. This is distinct from substances with well-defined mechanisms of lethal toxicity (e.g., respiratory depression from classic opioids or hypertensive crisis from classic stimulants). As Eckhardt and Nickel (2023) have concluded, “Some case reports of kratom associated arrhythmia, including fatalities, have surfaced, but little is known of the mechanism of kratom-induced ventricular arrythmia nor the depth of the problem.” 40. Attributing causation to mitragynine is confounded by (a) Ms. Moller’s pre-existing cardiac condition noted in the coroner’s report, (b) the multiple empty liquor and prescription pill bottles (including Acyclovir, methylphenidate, hydrocodone/acetaminophen, and gabapentin) and drug paraphernalia found at the scene (see St. Tammany Parish Sheriff’s Office Incident Report), 7

I do not see any basis in the autopsy report or NMS labs assessment of mitragynine or 7-OH levels that suggest anything but relatively low levels as compared to those that are more likely to be associated with death (see Papsun et al. 2023; Henningfield, Grundmann, Huestis and Smith, 2026). The mitragynine level was determined to be 150 ng/mL by NMS Labs and 158 ng/mL by UCSF Clinical Toxicology. NMS did not report 7-OH. UCSF Clinical Toxicology reported 0.8 ng/mL with a footnote indicating the “[v]alue was below the lower limit of quantification of 3 ng/mL and equal to the limit of detection for the analysis.” 42. Huestis et al, 2024 assessed the effects of single and consecutive daily oral ascending doses of dried kratom leaf powder in healthy adults, including the mitragynine and 7- OH concentrations, over 10 days after a single dose and 23 days after multiple dosing. This was a Health Canada approved study designed to detect kratom-related adverse effects. In the trial’s highest dose group (4000mg kratom leaf powder / 53.2mg mitragynine daily for 15 days), the mean steady state peak plasma concentration (Cmax) measured was 143 ng/mL with a median of 155 ng/mL (range 64.3 – 215 ng/mL). In this same group, the mean 7-OH level measured was 21- 8 ng/mL (range 13.3 – 31.7 ng/mL). The study concluded that the kratom powder was well- tolerated with no clinically significant abnormal findings in blood pressure, heart rate, or ECG. No active participants had abnormal QTc intervals, and QTc intervals greater than 500 milliseconds were not reported. 43. Reissig et al., 2024 evaluated the pharmacokinetics, pharmacodynamics, and safety of single ascending oral doses of botanical kratom in non-dependent, recreational polydrug users with opioid experience. In this pilot, placebo-controlled, dose-finding study performed under an Investigational New Drug (IND) application, participants were administered single doses of 1g, 3g, 8g, 10g, or 12g of oral kratom powder in capsules. In the highest dose groups, Cmax for mitragynine ranged from 250-300 ng/mL but 7-OH levels were below the lower limit of quantitation. The study concluded that at the doses tested, kratom was well-tolerated with no serious adverse effects reported, including no abnormalities in vital signs and ECG. 44. Smith et al., 2024 assessed the acute effects of a “typical” morning dose of kratom in 10 adults who use kratom regularly. This was an observational study designed to measure physiological, subjective, and psychomotor effects and to quantify alkaloids in plasma. Participants self-administered their typical dose of kratom (mean 5.16 g, range 1.1-10.9g). The mean plasma concentration for mitragynine found was 175.6 ng/mL (median 174.5 ng/mL, range 36.6 – 396.5 ng/mL). The mean plasma concentration for 7-OH was 34.0 ng/mL (median 27.4 ng/mL, range 2.9 – 77.7 ng/mL). The study concluded that among these regular consumers, there were “few clinically significant differences” pre- and post-dosing. Physiological changes, 8

ADDITIONAL EVIDENCE-BASED SUPPORT FOR OPINIONS Opinion 1: Kratom is not and should not be characterized as “an opioid,” nor regulated as a dangerous or addictive controlled substance in the U.S., CSA or under the International Drug Control Conventions of the United Nations. I agree with the determinations of the DEA and UNODC that kratom does not warrant such designations or control. 49. Kratom is not an opioid or narcotic by nature of its botanical origin, chemical structure or overall pharmacology and thus it is not included in the CSA or any of the United Nations International Drug Control Treaties. Nor has it ever been listed as a national drug threat in DEA’s annual National Drug Threat Assessment reports as necessary to meet statutory requirements for CSA Scheduling. Furthermore, kratom does not produce opioid-like respiratory depressant effects or the powerful euphoria that fuels the opioid epidemic. Its primary alkaloid and metabolites that do have some activity similar to opioids are partial agonists, meaning that their strongest effects are weaker than classic opioids (Henningfield et al. 2018, 2022, 2024; Kruegel et al. 2019; Kruegel et al., 2016; Henningfield and Fant, 2016; Varadi et al. 2016). 50. The DEA, NIDA, the U.S. Assistant Secretary for Health, and the WHO’s Expert Committee on Drug Dependence all agree with the conclusion that kratom is not an “opioid” and should not be scheduled as such. 51. In recent years, the FDA has been reevaluating its 2017 and 2018 statements that had suggested kratom had narcotic opioid-like effects. The FDA’s stated position as of December 2023 was that it “ha[d] not yet made a determination regarding whether kratom is dangerous.” (United States v. Although the FDA or DEA theoretically could determine that kratom and its constituents are sufficiently pharmacologically equivalent to previously scheduled drugs such as morphine-like opioids or methamphetamine-like stimulants, the scientific evidence does not support that conclusion. In 2017, the FDA developed an 8-factor analysis to support such a conclusion, but based on limitations in the evidence cited and because the agency ignored key evidence to the contrary, the FDA’s analysis was not considered reliable or valid by leading experts (e.g., Henningfield et al. 2018; US DHHS (Giroir, 2018) or the WHO Expert Committee on Drug Dependence, 2021). 53. Furthermore, in the FDA’s 2017 8-factor analysis, the agency ignored the serious adverse public health consequences of banning kratom and the benefits of keeping kratom available as a path away from opioid overdose. These considerations are a critical part of drug scheduling considered in factors 4, 5 and 6 of CSA 8-factor analysis as noted in DHHS’s review of the FDA’s analysis led by Assistant Secretary Giroir. Dr. Giroir stated, the “FDA’s recommendation was rejected because of embarrassingly poor evidence and data, and a failure to consider overall public health” (Giroir, 2021; and detailed analysis in Giroir, 2018). The DHHS report raised additional concerns, including the risk of precipitating potentially thousands of opioid overdose deaths, deterring kratom users (including pregnant women) from discussing their use with health care providers, the impact of criminalizing millions of U.S. citizens, and impeding further necessary research. 54. Separate from the DHHS report, I earlier led development of the first CSA guided 8-factor analysis to evaluate kratom’s potential for abuse (Pinney Associates, Henningfield and Fant, 2016). In summary, we concluded that factors 4, 5, and 61 weighed against scheduling and that there was not sufficient evidence of factors 1-3 or 7 to recommend scheduling. We further concluded that kratom and kratom constituents did not meet the factor 8 standard. 55. When the FDA’s 2017 8-factor analysis became publicly available, I also led a more detailed evaluation of the FDA analysis, along with eleven other leaders in kratom and opioid sciences and abuse potential. Our conclusions are summarized below: FDA’s 8-Factor Analysis does not constitute a reliable and valid scheduling decision guiding document. 1 Factors 4, 5 and 6 pertain to whether a substance with potential abuse-related uses poses a national drug threat and might warrant consideration for CSA scheduling. The factors are as follows: Factor 4: its history and current pattern of abuse; Factor 5: the scope, duration, and significance of abuse; and Factor 6: what, if any, risk is there to public health. 10

My review has been updated, peer-reviewed and published in 2018, and again in 2023 based on additional research (Henningfield et al. 2018, 2022, see also 2024). Those reviews include hundreds of new studies and additional reviews by other kratom research leaders who came to similar conclusions. 57. Kratom is in the same family as coffee, and like its botanical cousin, kratom contains many substances referred to as alkaloids, which tend to be somewhat alkaline and bitter in flavor. More than 40 alkaloids are identified in kratom to date, with most having little or no known pharmacological effect, or occurring at such low levels as to be of little cause for harm or benefit. The main ingredient in kratom currently thought to account for most of the pharmacological effects reported by consumers is mitragynine, which does not have strong rewarding and addictive effects like conventional stimulants, nor respiratory depressant effects like opioids (Brown et al. 2017; Henningfield, Grundmann, Huestis & Smith, 20204; McCurdy et al. 2024). 58. Unsurprisingly, given its botanical origin, kratom leaf products and extracts that contain primarily mitragynine are consumed by many people in place of coffee for alerting and occupational performance enhancing benefits (Henningfield et al. 2024). Another example of the distinction between kratom and narcotic like opioids. The term “narcotic” is derived from the Greek word for “stupor” and used to describing the sedating, sleepiness inducing, and sometimes dulling-of-the-senses effects of opioids. 59. To summarize, available scientific research has determined kratom does not have narcotic opioid-like properties. Opinion 2: Kratom is not characterized by “high abuse” potential. 60.
